metadata.title: Little and often: Causal inference machine learning demonstrates the benefits of homework for improving achievement in mathematics and science

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eighth-grade microdata for Ireland and applies the sampling weights derived from TIMSS’s stratified two-stage cluster design (complete classes sampled within schools). The authors state that these sampling weights were fully accounted for in the analysis by appropriately weighting results, which is consistent with producing nationally representative estimates for the Irish eighth-grade population. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty is presented via Bayesian credible intervals rather than replicate-based standard errors. For the analytic sample, the study focuses on the Irish eighth-grade subset (N=4118) and uses hierarchical modeling (random intercept) to reflect the student-within-school structure; missing values are handled via imputation rather than listwise deletion in the main analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Irish eighth-grade subset of TIMSS 2019 (seventh cycle), focusing on students’ mathematics and science homework frequency and duration from the student questionnaire and achievement from the TIMSS rotated booklet assessment. The analysis targets the eighth-grade mathematics and science outcomes and applies the TIMSS sampling weights; the main analysis retains students with missing values by imputing missing entries (6% missing) rather than restricting to complete cases.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Ireland) — homework frequency ATE
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) — ATE on TIMSS scale: Every day vs up to 1–2 times/week = 7.51 (95% credible interval 1.63 to 16.57); 3–4 times/week vs up to 1–2 times/week = 2.88 (−3.61 to 10.88). Scaled version (SD units): Every day = 0.10 (0.02 to 0.23); 3–4 times/week = 0.04 (−0.05 to 0.15).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Ireland) the study leveraged homework frequency category alongside math instructional time and student/family and school context variables to estimate mathematics achievement under counterfactual homework regimes, finding that increasing homework frequency to every day produced a positive causal average treatment effect (ATE) of 7.51 points on the TIMSS scale (95% credible interval 1.63–16.57). This indicates that structuring mathematics homework as frequent short assignments may causally improve mathematics achievement for Irish eighth graders, though effects are conditional on the model’s causal assumptions and the observational nature of treatment assignment.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Ireland) — homework frequency ATE
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) — ATE on TIMSS scale: 3–4 times/week vs up to 1–2 times/week = 5.34 (2.35 to 8.25); Every day vs up to 1–2 times/week = −1.94 (−5.96 to 2.28). Scaled version (SD units): 3–4 times/week = 0.07 (0.03 to 0.10); Every day = −0.02 (−0.07 to 0.03).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Ireland) the study leveraged homework frequency category alongside science instructional time and student/family and school context variables to estimate science achievement under counterfactual homework regimes, finding that the optimal frequency was 3–4 times per week (ATE = 5.34, 95% credible interval 2.35–8.25) while every-day homework showed no clear benefit (ATE = −1.94, −5.96 to 2.28). This indicates that science homework policy should target moderate weekly frequency rather than maximizing frequency, though causal interpretation depends on the BCF identification assumptions and unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Ireland) — homework duration ATE
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) — ATE on TIMSS scale (reference: up to 15 min each time): 16–30 minutes vs up to 15 min = −0.98 (−3.85 to 1.94); >30 minutes vs up to 15 min = 0.12 (−3.37 to 3.72). Scaled version (SD units): 16–30 minutes = −0.01 (−0.05 to 0.03); >30 minutes = 0.00 (−0.05 to 0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (Ireland) the study leveraged homework duration category alongside math instructional time and student/family and school context variables to estimate mathematics achievement under counterfactual homework regimes, finding no clear causal benefit to extending homework duration beyond 15 minutes per assignment (ATEs: −0.98 for 16–30 minutes and 0.12 for >30 minutes, both with credible intervals overlapping 0). This indicates that mathematics homework policy can prioritize short, frequent tasks over longer assignments without sacrificing achievement gains, while recognizing that the analysis is limited to frequency/duration and not homework quality.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Ireland) — homework duration ATE
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) — ATE on TIMSS scale (reference: up to 15 min each time): 16–30 minutes vs up to 15 min = 1.80 (−1.37 to 5.32); >30 minutes vs up to 15 min = 3.27 (−2.20 to 9.30). Scaled version (SD units): 16–30 minutes = 0.02 (−0.02 to 0.06); >30 minutes = 0.04 (−0.03 to 0.11).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Science (Ireland) the study leveraged homework duration category alongside science instructional time and student/family and school context variables to estimate science achievement under counterfactual homework regimes, finding insufficient evidence that longer homework durations increase science achievement (credible intervals for 16–30 minutes and >30 minutes overlap 0). This indicates that science homework policy may focus on keeping each assignment relatively short (around up to 15 minutes) while adjusting frequency, though causal claims remain conditional on the BCF assumptions and the study’s limited homework characterization.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics & Science (Ireland) — socioeconomic moderation
main_findings.target_variable: Homework effect heterogeneity by socioeconomic resources
main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderation results (Fig. 4) — no clear trend in predicted individual treatment effects by number of books at home or parents’ education level; effect magnitudes are approximately similar across socioeconomic groups in both subjects and at both frequencies.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 Mathematics and Science (Ireland) the study leveraged home educational resources (books at home) and parental education alongside homework frequency and duration to assess whether treatment effects differ by socioeconomic background, finding no clear evidence that advantaged students benefit more from homework than their peers. This indicates that, at least for Irish eighth graders, well-designed homework frequency/duration policies may improve achievement without widening socioeconomic achievement gaps, though the analysis cannot address homework quality or all potential unmeasured confounding.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses TIMSS 2019 seventh-cycle data, focusing on the Irish Grade 8 subset (N=4118) and modeling mathematics and science achievement using a multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests (BCF) approach. Homework is operationalized from student questionnaires as frequency (never to every day) and duration (up to 15 minutes to more than 90 minutes), with counterfactual average treatment effects (ATEs) estimated relative to reference categories. The authors pool five TIMSS plausible values for achievement by fitting separate models per PV and combining results, and they account for TIMSS’s stratified two-stage cluster sampling weights. Missing data (6%) are imputed using missRanger in the main analysis. Results show that mathematics achievement benefits most from every-day homework (ATE=7.51, 95% CrI 1.63–16.57), science from 3–4 times per week (ATE=5.34, 2.35–8.25), while extending duration beyond 15 minutes shows no clear benefit in either subject. The causal interpretation depends on BCF’s assumptions and on measured confounding; effects are also limited to frequency/duration rather than homework quality.
